paras: The killing of William Williams was the fatal shooting of an elderly Black farmhand by J. Z. Dodson, the white overseer of C. M. Cunningham's plantation on the Ogeechee River near Burroughs station, Georgia, on August 10, 1895. A coroner's jury ruled it accidental, but Williams's brother charged that Dodson had tried to kill him before, and Black residents threatened Dodson.
According to his brother John Cuthbert, Williams had been foreman of the place for twenty years and Dodson, a newcomer, had shot at him a year earlier.

At dusk on payday, Williams set his double-barrel breech-loader down on Dodson's piazza while they talked about guarding the watermelon patch. Dodson picked up the gun, was told it was not loaded, and both barrels discharged into Williams's side; he died within about ten minutes. As Black neighbors gathered and threatened his life, Dodson went to Savannah and reported the killing to Coroner Goette.

The next morning about a dozen Black men at the depot had Policeman Counihan arrest Dodson for murder until the coroner reclaimed him. On the testimony of Williams's sister Mary Wiley, a jury of four white and two Black men unanimously found the killing accidental. Cuthbert said Dodson had vowed to kill Williams, that Black witnesses feared being discharged, and that he would go to the grand jury.
Within days several Black residents were jailed for smashing watermelons on the plantation, while Dodson resumed charge; no grand jury action was reported.

The Savannah Morning News, the only paper found to cover the case, headed its first report "Forgot It Was Loaded," giving Dodson's account as fact. Its inquest story, "Wanted to Lynch Dodson," centered on Black anger while printing Cuthbert's accusation, and a later item, "Destroying the Crops," covered the arrests; no Black-press report was found.

The first report, from Dodson's side, said the dying man blamed himself for forgetting the gun was loaded. The sister testified that Williams made no statement about the shooting and only asked that a man pray for him.

reader.title: Killing of William Williams
bases: A white overseer shot a Black farmhand with the man's own gun; a coroner's jury ruled it accidental and only the victim's brother alleged intent, so no mob, band or officers were involved in the killing (A1, A2).

All three reports come from one paper, the Savannah Morning News; they agree that Dodson shot Williams, but the only version of intent beyond Dodson's and the sister's is the brother's statement to its reporter (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: Dodson's account (first report)
accounts.gist: The gun went off as Dodson unbreeched it after Williams said it was not loaded; the dying man blamed his own mistake.

accounts.label: Sister's testimony and coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Dodson saw two shells, snapped the gun shut and both exploded because the gun was not at safety; Williams made no statement about the shooting; the jury found it accidental.

accounts.label: Brother John Cuthbert
accounts.gist: Dodson had shot at Williams in the same house a year earlier and had told several people he meant to kill him; the trouble was that Dodson, a newcomer, could not get along with the long-time foreman.

framing.detail: The Morning News called it an 'accidental killing' from the first headline ('Forgot It Was Loaded'), took Dodson's and the jury's version, and framed the follow-ups around Black anger ('Wanted to Lynch Dodson', 'Destroying the Crops') while printing the brother's charge.
